definition.text: A naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure.

facts.text: A mineral differs from a rock: a rock is a bulk solid geologic material made of one mineral or an aggregate of several.
Natural solids with no definite crystal structure, such as opal or obsidian, are more properly called mineraloids.
One compound with two crystal structures counts as two species: quartz and stishovite are both silicon dioxide.
The International Mineralogical Association sets mineral names and definitions; as of August 2026 it recognizes 6,228 official mineral species.
To count as a mineral, a substance must form by natural geological processes, which excludes purely human-made or biological products such as seashells.
Silicate minerals make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust.
Minerals are classified by their key chemical constituents, chiefly in the Dana and Strunz systems.
In soil, the sand and silt fractions are mostly inert rock particles such as quartz, calcite, feldspar and mica.

definition.text: How the abundance of elements in the Earth's crust, and the swapping of one ion for another, control which minerals exist and how varied they are.

facts.text: Eight elements make up over 98% of the crust by weight: oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron, magnesium, calcium, sodium and potassium, in decreasing order.
Oxygen forms 47% of the crust by weight and silicon 28%.
The minerals that form are those most stable at the temperature and pressure of formation, within the limits set by the bulk chemistry.
Ions substitute for one another only when close in size and charge; Al3+ commonly replaces Si4+, as the two are similar in charge, size and crustal abundance.
In silicates, putting Al3+ in place of Si4+ leaves a charge to balance, which is why so many different silicate minerals exist.
Weathering or hydrothermal alteration changes a rock's composition, and with it the minerals the rock contains.

definition.text: Minerals built from the silicon–oxygen tetrahedron, [SiO4]4−, grouped by how far those tetrahedra link together.

facts.text: Silicon almost always sits in four-fold, tetrahedral coordination with oxygen.
Tetrahedra polymerize to different degrees, forming one-dimensional chains, two-dimensional sheets and three-dimensional frameworks.
Subclasses run from isolated tetrahedra (orthosilicates) through paired tetrahedra, rings and chains to sheets (phyllosilicates) and frameworks sharing all four corners (tectosilicates).
Al3+ often replaces Si4+ in the tetrahedra because the two ions have similar radius and charge, which changes how the structure's charge must be balanced.
Single-chain silicates are mostly pyroxenes and double-chain silicates often amphiboles; pyroxenes make up about 10% of the crust.
Silicates make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust.
Partial melting, crystallization, metamorphism, weathering and diagenesis have formed and reworked them for billions of years, and organisms such as diatoms also take part.

definition.text: Silicate minerals whose tetrahedra share all four corners, the most polymerized class, including quartz and the feldspars.

facts.text: Strong covalent bonds make framework silicates particularly stable chemically; quartz, 12% of the crust, is the most abundant mineral species and highly resistant.
A rock rich in quartz is considered mature, because quartz is the primary mineral that survived heavy weathering.
Feldspars are the most abundant mineral group in the crust; Al3+ substituting for Si4+ is balanced by added cations such as potassium, sodium or calcium.
Weathering of feldspar is a common source of clay minerals.

conflicts.text: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust by weight.
conflicts.note: Mineral gives about 50% (S:e1e4d91ec5bb) for the same share of the crust.

definition.text: Sheet silicates: minerals made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra, a class that includes the mica, chlorite and kaolinite–serpentine groups.

facts.text: Each tetrahedron is bound at three oxygen sites, giving a silicon to oxygen ratio of 2:5.
A sheet of octahedra balances the negatively charged tetrahedral sheet; these tetrahedral (T) and octahedral (O) sheets stack into layers.
The 1:1 clay minerals, the kaolinite–serpentine group, are T-O stacks held by hydrogen bonds; the 2:1 clay minerals are T-O-T stacks held by weaker van der Waals forces.
Micas are also T-O-T stacks but put aluminium in the tetrahedral sheets, whereas clay minerals hold Al3+ in octahedral sites; metal ions bond mica layers, making them harder.
Weak bonds between layers give phyllosilicates a prominent basal cleavage, so they split into thin, flexible flakes.
Octahedral sheets with every site filled are trioctahedral; those with some sites empty are dioctahedral, as in kaolinite and pyrophyllite.

definition.text: Minerals whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−, chiefly calcite, aragonite and dolomite.

facts.text: All carbonates react with acid, so field geologists carry dilute hydrochloric acid to tell carbonates from other minerals.
Calcite, CaCO3, is the most common carbonate and the main constituent of limestone and marble; dolomite is the double carbonate CaMg(CO3)2.
Carbonates usually form as biogenic or chemical sediments in marine settings.
Weathering of primary minerals by dissolved carbon dioxide, sometimes called carbonation, can produce secondary carbonate minerals.

definition.text: Minerals in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, divided into simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides.

facts.text: Hematite (Fe2O3) and corundum (Al2O3) belong to the corundum group of simple oxides.
Bauxite, the chief aluminium ore, is a mixture of hydroxides including gibbsite that forms where chemical weathering is very intense.
Magnetite is strongly magnetic because it holds iron in two oxidation states, Fe2+ and Fe3+.
Water converts many primary minerals to clay minerals or hydrated oxides through reactions called hydrolysis.

definition.text: Minerals that contain the sulfate anion, [SO4]2−, of which gypsum is by far the most common hydrous member.

facts.text: Sulfates commonly form as evaporites, precipitating from evaporating saline waters.
They also occur in hydrothermal veins or as oxidation products of sulfide minerals.
Gypsum, CaSO4·2H2O, forms with other evaporites such as calcite and halite; its anhydrous counterpart is anhydrite.

definition.text: The mineral species and groups that are far more abundant in rocks than the rest.

facts.text: A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids.
The main rock-forming minerals are quartz, the feldspars, micas, amphiboles, pyroxenes, olivines and calcite; all but calcite are silicates.
Some rocks are mostly one mineral, such as limestone (calcite) or quartzite (quartz); others, like granite, are defined by the proportions of key minerals.
Rocks can also be non-mineral: coal is a sedimentary rock made mainly of organically derived carbon.

definition.text: Telling minerals apart by physical properties such as crystal habit, hardness, lustre, colour, streak, cleavage and specific gravity.

facts.text: Some minerals can only be classified by optical, chemical or X-ray diffraction analysis, which can be costly and time-consuming.
Hardness is most often measured on the Mohs scale of scratch resistance, which runs through ten indicator minerals from talc to diamond.
Colour is the most obvious property but often not diagnostic; the streak, the colour of the powdered mineral, is independent of trace elements and weathering.
Even grains too small to see have a periodic crystal structure that X-ray diffraction can determine.

title: Biogenic minerals debate

definition.text: The dispute among geologists and mineralogists over the International Mineralogical Association's exclusion of crystalline substances made by living things.

facts.text: Lowenstam (1981) argued that organisms form a diverse array of minerals, some of which cannot form inorganically.
Skinner (2005) counts biominerals, created by organisms' metabolism, as minerals, and allows a mineral to be crystalline or amorphous.
Over 60 biominerals had been named before the IMA's listing, yet they are not on its official list of mineral names.
Mineral-forming microorganisms live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface, can precipitate metals from solution and can catalyse mineral dissolution.

contested_note: Mineralogists disagree over whether minerals made by organisms should count as minerals, which the IMA definition excludes.

definition.text: A fine-grained natural soil material containing clay minerals, the hydrous aluminium phyllosilicates such as kaolinite.

facts.text: Pure clay minerals are mostly white or pale, but impurities colour natural clays; small amounts of iron oxide give red or brown tones.
Clays become plastic when wet and can be hardened by firing.
Clay soils drain poorly, which makes them generally less suited to crops, but they are more fertile because of their higher cation-exchange capacity.
Mixtures of sand, silt and less than 40% clay are called loam.
Soils rich in swelling clays, which expand as they absorb water, are a major challenge in civil engineering.
Shale, formed largely from clay, is the most common sedimentary rock.
Clay is the longest-known ceramic raw material; some of the earliest pottery shards date to around 14,000 BCE.

definition.text: The making of clay minerals, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into clay deposits.

facts.text: Chemical weathering works largely by acid hydrolysis, driven by weak carbonic acid in rainwater or released by plant roots.
The acid breaks bonds between aluminium and oxygen, releasing other metal ions and silica as a gel of orthosilicic acid.
Orthoclase feldspar in granite weathers to kaolinite and silicic acid, releasing potassium ions.
Source rock and climate decide the product: feldspar-rich rock gives kaolin under warm acid weathering and illite under alkaline conditions.
Smectite forms from igneous rock under alkaline conditions, while gibbsite forms by intense weathering of other clay minerals.
Clay minerals can also form locally from hydrothermal activity.
Primary clays stay where they formed as residual soil deposits; secondary clays are carried off by water erosion and laid down elsewhere, often in large lakes or marine basins.

definition.text: The main kinds of clay, grouped by their dominant clay minerals: kaolinite, montmorillonite–smectite and illite.

facts.text: Chlorite, vermiculite, talc and pyrophyllite are sometimes also classed as clay minerals.
There are about 30 types of pure clay, but most natural deposits mix several of them with other weathered minerals.
Clay minerals are most easily identified by X-ray diffraction rather than by chemical or physical tests.
Varved clay shows visible annual layers laid down seasonally, and is common in former glacial lakes.

definition.text: The shaping and firing of clay into pottery and construction products, and its use in many industrial processes.

facts.text: Some of the earliest pottery shards, from central Honshu in Japan and linked to the Jōmon culture, date to around 14,000 BCE.
Ancient Mesopotamians adopted clay tablets, inscribed in cuneiform, as the first known writing medium.
Different clays, minerals and firing conditions produce earthenware, stoneware and porcelain.
Industry uses clay in paper making, cement production and chemical filtering, and as a filler in pencil lead.

definition.text: The use of clay, the defining ingredient of loam, as one of the oldest building materials on Earth.

facts.text: Between one-half and two-thirds of the world's population still live or work in buildings made with clay, often baked into brick.
Being relatively impermeable, clay seals pond linings, dam cores and landfill barriers against toxic seepage.
Clay served as mortar in brick chimneys and stone walls where protected from water.
Early 21st-century studies have tested clay's absorption capacity for removing heavy metals from waste water and purifying air.

title: Soil organic matter

definition.text: The organic part of soil: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, the cells and tissues of soil microbes, and the substances those microbes make.

facts.text: Most upland topsoils hold 1% to 6% organic matter by mass; deserts have under 1%, while low-lying wet soils can reach 90%.
It has three parts: living microbial biomass, fresh and partly decomposed detritus, and more stable organic carbon sometimes called humus; fresh surface litter is usually excluded.
It improves soil structure, aggregation, water retention, biodiversity, pollutant retention, buffering capacity and the cycling and storage of plant nutrients.
It raises fertility by supplying cation exchange sites and a store of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and micronutrients that mineralization slowly releases.
Organic matter is usually estimated to be 58% carbon, so measured soil organic carbon often serves as a proxy for it.
Soils containing 12% to 18% organic carbon are generally classed as organic soils.
How much organic matter builds up, and of what kind, depends on soil type, which the soil-forming factors control.

distinct_from: Soil organic matter in the carbon cycle

title: Soil organic carbon with depth
article: Soil organic matter#SOC distribution with depth

definition.text: How the amount, age and makeup of soil organic carbon change between the surface layer, roughly the top 20 cm, and the deeper mineral soil.

facts.text: About 70% of global soil organic carbon lies deeper than 20 cm.
Surface soil has higher carbon concentrations, but deeper soil stores more carbon overall because of its greater mass.
Radiocarbon dates show carbon growing older with depth, a sign that deep soil stores it for longer.
Living things shape organic carbon near the surface, while mineral influences dominate at depth, through mineral-associated organic matter.

distinct_from: Soil organic matter in the carbon cycle

title: Mineral-associated organic matter

definition.text: Soil organic matter chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces.

facts.text: It is thought to consist of small plant and microbial molecules bonded to charged mineral surfaces or locked inside aggregates.
Binding to minerals makes it harder for decomposers to reach, so it resists microbial breakdown and loss from the soil carbon pool.
It typically persists for centuries, whereas particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.

notes: No page or section of its own; defined on Soil carbon and discussed in Soil organic matter#SOC distribution with depth (mentioned on two in-scope pages).

title: Composition of plant residues

definition.text: The water, elements and organic compounds that make up the plant debris from which soil organic matter forms.

facts.text: Plant debris is 60% to 90% water.
Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen make up about 92% of the dry weight; the rest includes nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium and micronutrients.
Its organic compounds include carbohydrates from simple sugars to cellulose, fats, lignins from older woody parts, and proteins containing nitrogen.
Charcoal, elemental carbon left by incomplete burning, is highly resistant to decomposition.

distinct_from: Soil organic matter in the carbon cycle

title: Soil organic matter in the carbon cycle
article: Soil organic matter#Function in carbon cycling

definition.text: The role of soil organic matter as a large carbon store that can act as either a sink or a source of carbon.

facts.text: The global soil carbon pool is estimated at 2,500 gigatons, 3.3 times the atmospheric pool of 750 gigatons and 4.5 times the biotic pool of 560 gigatons.
Organic carbon, mostly as soil organic matter, accounts for about 1,550 gigatons; the rest is soil inorganic carbon, mainly carbonates and bicarbonates.
Gains and losses keep the pool in dynamic equilibrium, so soil can take up carbon by sequestration or release it as greenhouse gas emissions.
Because soil can hold carbon for centuries to millennia, organic matter management matters for climate change mitigation.

notes: Overlaps the Soil carbon entry of soil-carbon-and-climate; merge there if the duplicates pass prefers one.

title: Climate and organic matter accumulation

definition.text: The strong control that climate, chiefly temperature and moisture, exerts on how organic matter is produced, built up and broken down in soil.

facts.text: Temperature, soil moisture and topography are the main factors in how much organic matter accumulates.
Organic matter builds up where cold or waterlogging, which makes soil anaerobic, slows decomposers.
Heavy rain and heat in the tropics speed decomposition and nutrient leaching, so forests there depend on efficient recycling of nutrients by living biomass.
Steep slopes under cultivation encourage erosion of the topsoil, which holds most of the raw organic material that would otherwise become humus.

distinct_from: Soil organic matter in the carbon cycle

definition.text: The quality of a soil set by its make-up of sand, silt and clay particles.

facts.text: Texture considers only particles less than two millimetres across, namely sand, silt and clay.
Texture classes rest on the percentages of sand, silt and clay; the USDA and WRB systems use 12 classes and the UK-ADAS system 11.
It can be judged qualitatively, by texture by feel, or measured quantitatively, for example by the hydrometer method based on Stokes' law.
Texture is fixed by a soil's mineral component and does not change with farming, unlike soil structure.
Field capacity, the soil water content best suited to plant growth, rises as soil particles get finer, from sand to clay.
Texture helps decide which crops suit a soil and predicts its response to drought or its lime needs.
Albert Atterberg proposed the first texture classification, the international system, in 1905.

definition.text: The breakdown of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living things.

facts.text: Weathering happens in place, which sets it apart from erosion, where water, ice, wind, waves or gravity carry rock and mineral material away.
It is either physical, the mechanical breakdown of rock by heat, water, ice and wind, or chemical, the reaction of rock with water, gases and biological chemicals.
Water drives both kinds, though atmospheric oxygen and carbon dioxide and the activities of organisms also matter.
The material left after rock breaks down combines with organic material to create soil.
The two kinds work together: cracks widened physically expose more surface to chemical attack, speeding disintegration.
Weathering is a crucial part of the rock cycle; sedimentary rock, made from weathered rock, covers 66% of the continents.

definition.text: Weathering that breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry; also called mechanical weathering or disaggregation.

facts.text: Most of it comes from expansion and contraction with temperature change, as in freeze–thaw and thermal fracturing; pressure release works without any temperature change.
It is usually much less important than chemical weathering, but can be significant in subarctic or alpine settings.
Frost weathering is its most important form, followed by wedging by plant roots that enter cracks and pry them apart.
Burrowing worms and other animals, and plucking by lichens, can also help break rock apart.

title: Frost weathering

definition.text: Physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops.

facts.text: Water expands 9.2% on freezing; a realistic upper limit on the pressure is 14 megapascals, far above granite's tensile strength of about 4 megapascals.
Frost wedging, long thought the main mechanism, needs small tortuous cracks in almost saturated rock, conditions unusual enough that it is unlikely to dominate.
In ice segregation, water drawn to growing ice lenses can exert up to ten times the pressure of frost wedging; it works best between −4 and −15 °C.
It is strongest in alpine, periglacial, subpolar maritime and polar climates, but can occur anywhere between −3 and −8 °C if water is present.

contested_note: Frost wedging was long believed the main mechanism, but growing theoretical and experimental work favours ice segregation.

title: Thermal stress weathering

definition.text: Weathering caused by rock expanding and contracting as its temperature changes.

facts.text: It takes two forms: thermal shock, where rock cracks at once, which is uncommon, and the more typical thermal fatigue, where repeated stress cycles gradually weaken rock.
It matters in deserts with large day–night temperature swings, but any large temperature change, including wildfire, can drive it, so it is likely as important in cold climates.
It works best when heated rock is buttressed by surrounding rock and can expand in only one direction.
Geologists long discounted it after early 20th-century oven experiments, since criticized as unrealistic; geomorphologists now re-emphasize it.

contested_note: Its importance was long discounted on the basis of early experiments that have since been criticized as unrealistic.

definition.text: Physical weathering, also called unloading, that occurs when deeply buried rock is brought to the surface and the weight on it is removed.

facts.text: Granite and other intrusive rocks form deep underground under great pressure; when erosion strips the rock above, their outer parts expand.
The expansion opens fractures parallel to the surface, and sheets of rock break away along them, a process called exfoliation or sheeting.
In buttressed rock the stress toward the free surface can reach 35 megapascals, easily enough to shatter rock.
Retreat of an overlying glacier can also cause exfoliation by pressure release.

definition.text: The breaking up of rock when salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there; also called haloclasty.

facts.text: Like ice lenses, salt grains draw in more dissolved salt by capillary action and grow into lenses that press hard on the surrounding rock.
Sodium and magnesium salts are the most effective.
It occurs wherever evaporation concentrates salts, so it is most common in arid climates and along coasts.
Weathering of pyrite to iron(II) sulfate and gypsum can also grow salt lenses in sedimentary rock.

definition.text: Weathering in which water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition.

facts.text: Most rock forms at high temperature and pressure, so its minerals are often unstable in the cool, wet, oxidizing conditions at the Earth's surface.
It turns some primary minerals into secondary minerals, carries other substances off in solution, and leaves the most stable minerals unchanged as a resistate.
The new set of minerals is closer to equilibrium with surface conditions, but true equilibrium is rare because leaching removes the dissolved products.
Water is the main agent, turning many primary minerals into clay minerals or hydrated oxides by hydrolysis; oxygen oxidizes minerals and carbon dioxide drives carbonation.
It is usually much more important than physical weathering.
Mountain uplift exposes fresh rock to air and moisture, releasing calcium and other ions into surface waters.

definition.text: Chemical weathering in which a mineral dissolves completely without leaving any new solid; also called simple or congruent dissolution.

facts.text: Rainwater easily dissolves soluble minerals such as halite and gypsum, and given enough time even quartz, which goes into solution as silicic acid.
In carbonate dissolution, rainwater and carbon dioxide form weak carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone into soluble calcium bicarbonate.
Cold water holds more dissolved carbon dioxide, so carbonate dissolution is favoured at low temperature and is important in glacial weathering.
Unpolluted rain has a pH of around 5.6; sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides make acid rain that can lower it to 4.5 or even 3.0.

definition.text: Chemical weathering in which only part of a mineral dissolves and the rest turns into a new solid such as a clay mineral; carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide.

facts.text: Most is acid hydrolysis: protons in acidic water attack the chemical bonds in mineral crystals.
Carbonic acid from dissolved carbon dioxide is the main source of protons, though organic acids also matter.
The weakest cation–oxygen bonds go first, so igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed, Bowen's reaction series; illite is unusually stable, silica unusually unstable.
Orthoclase feldspar, carbonic acid and water yield kaolinite, silicic acid, and potassium and bicarbonate ions in solution.
Carbonation can also turn primary minerals into secondary carbonate minerals, as when forsterite weathers to magnesite.
Silicate weathering consumes carbonic acid and leaves alkaline bicarbonate solutions, an important control on atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate.

definition.text: Chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+.

facts.text: Oxygen and water oxidize Fe2+ to Fe3+ oxides and hydroxides such as goethite, limonite and hematite.
This gives rock a reddish-brown surface that crumbles easily and weakens the rock.
Sulfide minerals oxidize too, as when chalcopyrite turns to copper hydroxide and iron oxides, leaving coloured deposits.
Oxidizing primary minerals, especially sulfides and those containing Fe2+, generates soil acidity.

definition.text: Chemical weathering in which water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral.

facts.text: Examples are iron oxides turning into iron hydroxides and anhydrite hydrating to gypsum.
Bulk hydration matters less than dissolution, hydrolysis and oxidation, but hydration of the crystal surface is the crucial first step in hydrolysis.
Water at a fresh surface splits into H+ and OH−; protons then replace surface cations, freeing them, and loosened bonds release silicic acid and aluminium hydroxides.
In the regolith, hydration turns silicate minerals such as feldspars into clay minerals; montmorillonite can take up varying water without changing its structure.

definition.text: Weathering started or sped up by living things, such as soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots.

facts.text: Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils; albite and muscovite weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil.
Lichens are among the most effective agents: hornblende granite under lichen weathered 3x–4x faster than bare rock in a New Jersey study.
Most commonly, plants release chelating compounds such as organic acids and siderophores, along with carbon dioxide.
Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases.
Chelating organic acids strip metal ions, especially aluminium and silicon, from rock; their build-up can lead to podsolisation of soils.
Mycorrhizal fungi free nutrients from minerals such as apatite or biotite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth.
Physically, seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae.

definition.text: The conversion of rock into soil material as weathering turns its minerals into clay minerals and iron oxides.

facts.text: Granite starts weathering with the loss of hornblende; biotite then becomes vermiculite, oligoclase and microcline go last, and all end as clay minerals and iron oxides.
Soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon compared with the bedrock.
It gains at least 50% in aluminium and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude.
Basalt weathers more easily than granite, being formed hotter and drier, fine-grained and glassy; it turns to potassium-poor montmorillonite, then kaolinite.
Continuous intense leaching, as in rain forests, ends in bauxite; intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in iron- and titanium-rich laterite.
Soil formation takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time.
The chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O), runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.

definition.text: A building block pressed from a fairly dry mix of inorganic subsoil, non-expansive clay, sand and aggregate.

facts.text: The damp mix is pressed at around 3,000 psi (21 MPa), roughly halving its volume, then dried; with cement added it becomes a stabilized earth block.
Unlike mud bricks, which harden by air-drying, the blocks are compressed, and properly made ones are usually stronger.
It was developed for low-cost building as an alternative to adobe.
Long contact with water weakens earth blocks and can make them disintegrate completely.

definition.text: Surface weathered rinds on ultramafic rocks in which nickel has been concentrated into ore.

facts.text: They hold 80% of the continental world's nickel resources.
They form by intense tropical weathering of olivine-rich rocks and serpentinite holding about 0.3% nickel, which lateritization strongly enriches.
Upper limonite ores are iron-rich goethite with 0.8–1.5% nickel, left by strong leaching of magnesium and silica; lower silicate ores hold 1.5–3% nickel in serpentine.
Nickel in the silicate zone is leached downward from the goethite zone above.

definition.text: The extraction of sand, mostly from open pits but also from beaches, inland dunes, and ocean and river beds.

facts.text: Sand goes into concrete, abrasives and icy roads, and mining can also recover rutile, ilmenite and zircon for titanium and zirconium.
Sand mining directly causes erosion and harms wildlife, coral and fisheries.
Globally a $70 billion industry, it is regulated in many places but often done illegally.
Illegal sand mining is a global resource-depletion problem comparable in extent to water scarcity.

definition.text: A carbonate mineral, the most stable polymorph of calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

facts.text: It is very common, particularly in limestone, and defines hardness 3 on the Mohs scale.
Acid dissolves it and releases carbon dioxide, giving a characteristic fizz.
Groundwater can dissolve or precipitate calcite depending on temperature, pH and dissolved ions; less dissolved carbon dioxide makes it precipitate.
Unusually, it becomes less soluble in water as temperature rises.

definition.text: The branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical, including optical, properties of minerals.

facts.text: It covers how minerals originate and form, how they are classified, where they occur and how they are used.
Minerals form in settings from igneous melts deep in the crust to the oxidation and weathering of rock at the surface or within soil.
Identification starts with physical properties measurable on a hand sample, such as hardness on the Mohs scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
X-ray diffraction, demonstrated in 1912, became a tool for analysing mineral crystal structures.

definition.text: A rigid microscopic mineral deposit, usually of silica, formed in plant tissue and often persisting after the plant decays.

facts.text: Plants take up dissolved silica from the soil as monosilicic acid, Si(OH)4, which can reach 0.1% to 10% of their dry weight.
Phytoliths can persist in soils for thousands of years and are abundant in the fossil record from the Late Devonian onwards.
They are used to identify palaeoenvironments and track vegetation change.
Carbon occluded in phytoliths resists decay for millennia and accumulates in soils, with stores that vary by species, biome, climate and soil.

definition.text: A discoloured, chemically altered outer layer of a rock fragment, formed by weathering.

facts.text: It forms on clasts from pebbles to boulders, at the surface or buried in alluvium, colluvium or till, through exposure to air or shallow groundwater.
Rinds are often enriched in iron, manganese and silica and oxidized to yellowish red or reddish colours.
Comparing rind thickness on gravel of similar rock gives relative ages of Quaternary deposits: thicker rinds mean older deposits.
Calibrated against radiocarbon-dated deposits, an age–thickness curve can date other deposits; the relation is taken to be logarithmic.
